body: Two things. Eucheuma cottonii, the warm-water seaweed the listing places off Tanzania, and water. No second alga, no preservative, no thickener and no sweetener is declared.
It is not the same plant as the Atlantic Chondrus crispus gel, and it is ten pounds cheaper because the plant is cheaper. Reiss puts the two side by side here.
One or two tablespoons a day, preferably in the morning, with a clean spoon.

Off the spoon, or blended into a smoothie. The listing gives the jar 20 days at one tablespoon and 10 days at two. If you miss a day, do not take double the next one: seaweed carries iodine and there is an upper limit on how much of it you want in a day.

body: How much gel is in the jar. The listing prints days of servings and never a volume or a fill weight, so this page prices a day and cannot compare the jar with anything else by size.

The listing also says cultivated off Tanzania in one line and wild crafted from Zanzibar in another. Zanzibar is part of Tanzania; farmed and wild are not. Until the label picks one, this sheet prints both.
Keep it in the fridge, which the listing prints, and use a clean spoon, which it also prints. Lid back on after each serving.
There is no shelf life in days on this listing. What it gives you is 20 days of spoons at one tablespoon a day.
Anyone pregnant or trying to conceive, and anyone taking blood related medication. That is the caution the listing carries and we carry it here as it stands.
Anyone with an overactive thyroid should leave it alone. If you take thyroid medication, ask your GP or pharmacist before you start, and keep it away from children.
Made and sent out from 599 Smithdown Road, Liverpool. Orders go out chilled, Tuesday to Sunday. UK delivery is free over £50, or you can collect from the shop between 10 and 6, any day except Monday.

ingredients.intro: The listing names one seaweed and describes the water it is prepared with. That is the whole of the declared list.

cards.p: The warm-water species, grown on lines strung between stakes in shallow lagoons off Tanzania. The branches are thick and round in section, closer to a knobbly coral than to the flat forking fans of the Atlantic plant, and the colour runs from pale gold to purple. Sold and farmed as Eucheuma cottonii; botanists more often place the farmed plant in Kappaphycus, as Kappaphycus alvarezii. The trade name is the one on the jar.
cards.none: of the species; nothing sourced has passed the checks

cards.alt: Thick golden wrack washed up on a beach
cards.p: The wrack in this photograph is not Eucheuma. It is here because it shows the round, glossy, pale form that Eucheuma has and that the flat forking Atlantic plant does not. The article puts the two side by side, dried and as a gel.

cards.alt: Glass and jug of water in morning light
cards.p: The seaweed is soaked and blended with water. The listing describes that water as filtered and hydrogen treated. That is a description of a process and this card carries it as one. Nothing else is declared: no second alga, no preservative, no thickener, no sweetener.

spec.label: Sea moss · the warm-water one
spec.intro: Everything we can tell you about what is in the jar, including the figure the listing leaves out and the line where it contradicts itself.
spec.caption: Purple Mwani Sea Moss Gel
rows: A single-species gel. One red alga, Eucheuma cottonii, prepared with water.
Eucheuma cottonii, the warm-water species. Botanists more often place the farmed plant in Kappaphycus, as Kappaphycus alvarezii. The listing uses the trade name and so does this sheet.
Mwani is Swahili for seaweed, and the listing says the word is used in particular for this species. Purple is the colour the plant runs to.

The listing says cultivated off Tanzania in one line and wild crafted from Zanzibar in another. Zanzibar is part of Tanzania; farmed and wild are not. Until the label picks one, this sheet prints both.
The alga and water. No second alga, no preservative, thickener or sweetener is declared.
Water. The listing describes it as filtered and hydrogen treated. That is a description of a process and this sheet carries it as one.
One jar, £24.99. The listing prints no volume. The 1000 g in the shop's variant data is a shipping weight rather than a fill weight, so this sheet carries no millilitre figure.
One or two tablespoons daily, preferably in the morning, with a clean spoon. Off the spoon, or blended into a smoothie.
As printed: 20 days at one tablespoon, 10 days at two. That works out at £1.25 a day at one tablespoon and £2.50 at two.
Sea moss contains iodine. The amount in a spoonful varies from harvest to harvest, so we do not print a per spoon figure. If you need to count iodine, Seaking is measured at 75 µg a capsule.
Refrigerate, as printed, and use a clean spoon, also as printed. The listing gives no shelf life in days for this jar; what it gives is 20 days of spoons at one tablespoon.
None. A gel needs no capsule shell, binder or flow agent.
Vegans. Adults. The declared list is a seaweed and water.

Anyone pregnant or trying to conceive, and anyone taking blood related medication. That is the caution the listing carries and we print it as it stands. Anyone with an overactive thyroid should leave it alone, and if you take thyroid medication ask your GP or pharmacist before you start. Not for children.
spec.smallprint: Contains iodine from seaweed. Do not exceed two tablespoons a day. Speak to your GP or pharmacist before starting any supplement, particularly if you have a thyroid condition or take medication for one. Food supplements should not be used as a substitute for a varied and balanced diet and a healthy lifestyle. Keep out of reach of young children.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: The species is named in Latin, the country is named, the serving and the days of spoons are printed, the cost a day follows from them, and the caution the listing carries is printed as it stands. The volume of the jar is missing and the sheet says so rather than guessing at it. What a spoonful does in the body is not something we are permitted to say, so it is not on this page.

reiss.label: Reiss's turn
reiss.h2: The cheaper plant, sold as the cheaper plant
paras: Most of what is sold in this country as Irish moss is this species. It is farmed on lines in warm shallow water off Tanzania, Zanzibar, the Philippines and Indonesia, and it costs a fraction of what hand-picked Atlantic Chondrus crispus costs. A good deal of it is then sold at Chondrus prices under a Chondrus name.

So here it is under its own name, at twenty four ninety nine, which is ten pounds under the plain Atlantic jar. Same shelf, different plant, different price. If you have bought sea moss online and it came out pale, stiff and glossy on the spoon, this is most likely what you bought, and you can work out for yourself whether what you paid was the price of this.

Our team went out to the mwani farms in 2020, which is where the word on the jar comes from. The row that annoys me is the volume: the listing says how many days of spoons are in the jar and never how much gel. That is enough to price a day and not enough to compare it with anything else on the shelf, and it is on the list to fix.
reiss.pull: It is the cheaper plant, and it is priced like the cheaper plant.
